paras: The lynching of John Brodie and Shadrack Hester took place in the early hours of December 1, 1881, at Oxford, Granville County, North Carolina, when a party of masked men took the two Black prisoners from the county jail and hanged them. Both men were held on a charge of murdering Thomas M. Lynch, an Oxford jeweler, and had not been tried. The Raleigh wire carried the story nationally the same day, and several North Carolina papers presented the hanging as just retribution.

According to the Oxford Free Lance, Lynch, a Presbyterian deacon and the town's only jeweler, was killed on a dark Tuesday night on the road home from his store, his skull fractured and his pocketbook with about $20 taken. The next morning suspicion fell on Shadrack Hester, who after telling "many different stories" confessed his part and charged John Brodie, recently released from the penitentiary, with striking the blow. In jail both men denied the crime, Hester saying he had lied, but before the coroner's jury he repeated his statement and the jury returned a "true bill."
A Raleigh dispatch of November 26 reported "strong talk of lynching" in Oxford and said a guard had been placed around the jail.

About 3 a.m. a body of disguised and armed men, numbering between fifty and one hundred, woke jailer Wm. R. Turner at his home and made him go with them to the jail. There they forced the two guards, Capt. A. F. Spencer and W. H. Crews, a Black constable, into the guard house at pistol point and put out the lamps. Hester was taken from his cell first, and Brodie, threatened with death if he raised an alarm, was allowed to dress and was marched out.

Around 8 a.m. the two bodies were found hanging on separate trees about twenty feet apart in a small grove in Taylor's field, roughly 150 yards from where Lynch had been killed. Hundreds of people came to look at the bodies.

An Oxford dispatch reported that "all is quiet" and that no trouble was expected over the lynching. No report of an inquest on the hanged men or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage. A postscript in the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic passed on a rumor that "at least half the Lynchers were colored men" and a report that the prisoners had confessed to a plot to kill Lynch and two other men. The Raleigh Observer, quoted in Charlotte, named the others as a Mr. Brogden and Mr. Clements, the county Register of Deeds.

The first national report was a Raleigh dispatch drawn from a News and Observer special, run on December 2 in papers from New York and Memphis to St. Paul and Sacramento. It said the victims had reportedly "made a full confession" and that everything "was conducted with the utmost secrecy." Headlines ranged from "Two Men Lynched" in Sacramento to "Two Murderers Well Hanged" in St. Paul; the New-York Tribune's "Four Negroes Lynched" joined the case to a Mississippi lynching of the same day. Weekly briefs through mid-December repeated it, some as "four negro murderers" or with the names garbled into "Louis Burke and John Booker."

North Carolina papers mostly approved. The Farmer and Mechanic headed the Free Lance account "Retribution!" and wrote that "vengeance overtook the assassins," while the Charlotte Home and Democrat called it "Speedy Justice." The Orange County Observer went further, suggesting that when guilt was sure it "might be better" to roast prisoners alive. A dissenting letter in the Charlotte Home and Democrat regretted "another case of lynching in North Carolina," asked who would guarantee that only the guilty would be hanged, and urged the press to oppose mob law.

Accounts put the party at fifty or sixty to about one hundred men, and the site at the murder spot itself (Knoxville) or a large oak on the western outskirts (Alexandria). The wire's report of a full confession contrasts with the Free Lance report that both denied the crime in jail, and a Raleigh dispatch's claim that Lynch's sons found two men dividing the money under a bridge is absent from the local account.

reader.title: Lynching of John Brodie and Shadrack Hester
bases: Two Black prisoners held on a murder charge were taken from the Oxford jail by a masked, armed party and hanged (A9, A20).

Brodie and Hester were hanged by a party of fifty to one hundred disguised men who forced the jailer to give them up, without any trial, because they were charged with the murder of Thomas M. Lynch (A20, A8, A24).

The Oxford Free Lance account reprinted in Raleigh (A20), the News and Observer special carried by the wire (A8, A9), and a separate Oxford dispatch (A13) agree that the two prisoners were taken from jail and hanged.

accounts.label: Oxford Free Lance (via Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic)
accounts.gist: Fifty to one hundred disguised armed men forced the jailer to open the jail, held the guard silent, took Hester and then Brodie from their cells, and hanged them on separate trees in a grove in Taylor's field near the murder spot.

accounts.label: News and Observer special / AP wire
accounts.gist: About 3 a.m. some 75 to 100 masked men took the two from the Oxford jail and hanged them in a small grove near the murder site; the victims were reported to have made a full confession.

accounts.label: Burke and Booker version
accounts.gist: Two men named 'Louis Burke and John Booker', charged with killing 'Charles Lynch', were taken by fifty or sixty men, confessed, begged for mercy and were hanged on the outskirts of the village.

framing.detail: The Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic headed the Free Lance account 'Retribution!' and wrote that 'vengeance overtook the assassins'.
The Orange County Observer called the men 'murderers' and said it might be better to 'roast them alive'.
The Charlotte Home and Democrat ran the news as 'SPEEDY JUSTICE' and called the men 'villains'.
The St. Paul Daily Globe headed the wire 'Two Murderers Well Hanged'.
A correspondent of the Charlotte Home and Democrat regretted 'another case of lynching in North Carolina' and called for opinion against 'any kind of mob law'.
Most papers outside the state ran the Raleigh wire under neutral heads such as 'Two Men Lynched' or 'Judge Lynch.', often paired with a Mississippi lynching.

conflicts.note: The local Free Lance account gives fifty to one hundred.
The Burke/Booker items give the same jail, town, jeweler and manner of death; they read as a garbled version of the same event, and the local papers use Brodie and Hester.
Four comes from combining the Oxford hangings with two in Mississippi on the same day (A8, A27).
